reason: The sources provide rich, verified details across multiple independent sites supporting a compelling 45-second script with 15 multi-sourced claims.
story: In October 1957, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev demanded a dramatic space spectacular to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution in under four weeks. Rocket designer Sergei Korolev rushed to assemble Sputnik 2, installing a stray Moscow street dog named Laika inside a hastily built cabin. Because re-entry technology did not exist, the mission was designed to be one-way. Scientists trained Laika in progressively smaller cages and monitored her vital signs during launch on November 3, 1957. For decades, official Soviet accounts claimed Laika survived several days in orbit before being painlessly euthanized. However, in 2002, mission scientist Dimitri Malashenkov revealed the truth: a failure in thermal control caused cabin temperatures to soar, killing Laika within five to seven hours from panic and overheating on her fourth orbit. Sputnik 2 burned up during re-entry on April 14, 1958, after 2,570 orbits.
angle: For 45 years, the Soviet government covered up Laika's true fate, claiming she lived for days in space when she actually died of intense heat and panic within hours.

claims.claim: Nikita Khrushchev requested a space mission to mark the 40th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution.
Soviet engineers had less than four weeks to design and construct Sputnik 2 for the November 1957 deadline.
Sputnik 3 was already under development but could not be completed in time for the anniversary.
Laika was a stray dog captured from the streets of Moscow.
Laika became the first animal to orbit the Earth when launched aboard Sputnik 2 in November 1957.
Three dogs were trained for the Sputnik 2 mission: Albina, Mushka, and Laika.
Albina served as the primary backup dog because she had previously flown high-altitude rocket tests.
Candidate dogs were kept in progressively smaller cages for up to 20 days to adapt them to the tiny cabin.
Laika was fed a special high-nutrition gel gelled with agar.
Chains and a harness restricted Laika's movement inside the capsule, preventing her from turning around.
The life-support system contained an oxygen generator, carbon dioxide absorber, and a cooling fan set to activate above 15 °C.
Medical sensors on Laika tracked her respiration, heartbeat, and blood pressure during flight.
In weightlessness, Laika's pulse took three times longer to return to resting levels than it did in ground centrifuge tests.
Official Soviet sources originally claimed Laika survived in orbit for several days or was painlessly euthanized.
In 2002, scientist Dimitri Malashenkov revealed Laika died within five to seven hours of launch from overheating and stress.
Sputnik 2 reentered Earth's atmosphere and burned up on April 14, 1958, after 2,570 orbits.

disputed: Laika's original name: Different sources report names including Kudryavka, Limonchik, Malyshka, and Zhuchka. Script should note she was originally called Kudryavka before being renamed Laika.

Electro-cardio signals on day two: A declassified 1957 letter suggested heart activity on day two, but historians point out orbital tracking gaps and thermal breakdown make this unreliable. Script should rely on the 2002 Malashenkov disclosure that she died on orbit four.
Initial launch time: Soviet launch records vary between 05:30:42 and 07:22 Moscow Time. Script should avoid giving a specific launch time minute.
